# Longitude by marine chronometer (`longitude_chronometer`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: needs mechanical_clock; helped by latitude_astrolabe_quadrant, precision_measurement
- Core idea: The Earth turns 15° an hour, so longitude is a time difference: carry a clock that keeps home-port time and compare it with local time from the Sun (noon, or a timed altitude); convert apparent solar time to mean time using the equation of time before comparing the readings; every four minutes of difference is one degree, every second about 460 m at the equator. To be useful the clock must keep a known rate to a few seconds a day through months of rolling, heat and cold; pendulums fail at sea, so it uses a balance wheel with temperature compensation (bimetal strips) and a detached escapement. Harrison's H4 lost only about five seconds on a voyage of 81 days to Jamaica (1761–62); Kendall's copy went round the world with Cook.
- Pitfalls:
  - Using a pendulum clock at sea
  - Thinking one perfect clock is enough; carry two or three and log each one's daily rate
  - Crediting the method to Harrison; Gemma Frisius proposed it in 1530, the problem was building the clock
  - Saying the chronometer replaced lunar distances at once; chronometers were expensive and both methods coexisted until the mid-19th c.
- History: europe: 1530 – Gemma Frisius proposes the clock method; 1714 Longitude Act offers £20,000; 1761–62 Harrison's H4 trial; 1772–75 Kendall's K1 on Cook's second voyage; 1780s Arnold and Earnshaw make affordable chronometers; Le Roy and Berthoud in France
- Read:
  - Rupert T. Gould, The Marine Chronometer: Its History and Development (1923)
  - Dava Sobel, Longitude (1995)
  - William J. H. Andrewes (ed.), The Quest for Longitude (1996)
